Para cuando terminó la entrada, Nolan Arenado ya había dado la vuelta a las bases, Arizona había anotado cinco veces y los Yankees se habían quedado atrás para siempre, acabando por perder 8-4 ante los Diamondbacks.
Con esta derrota, los Yankees quedan con un balance de 89-66 y a seis partidos de los Tampa Bay Rays, cuando solo quedan siete partidos por jugar. Además, esto puso fin a una gira por Arizona con un balance de 1-2, después de que Nueva York empezara la serie con una victoria por 9-2 y luego perdiera dos veces en partidos que se decidieron en los últimos compases.
Los Yankees ya se han asegurado una plaza en la postemporada y siguen ocupando el primer puesto de comodín de la Liga Americana. Pero la última semana tiene ahora un carácter de urgencia diferente. Tampa Bay puede hacerse con el título de la División Este de la Liga Americana con una sola victoria en la serie de cuatro partidos que empieza el martes en el Yankee Stadium.
El domingo también se prolongó el drástico cambio de rumbo tras el partido inaugural del viernes. El sábado terminó con un jonrón decisivo de Pavin Smith contra Michael Fulmer. El último partido trajo consigo otro fallo del bullpen, pero el mismo perjuicio en la clasificación.
Una entrada de cuatro carreras debería haber cambiado el rumbo de la tarde
Arizona se adelantó en el marcador gracias a un sencillo impulsador de Geraldo Perdomo en la primera entrada. A partir de ahí, Will Warren se asentó en el montículo, impidiendo que los Diamondbacks ampliaran su ventaja hasta la cuarta entrada y dando tiempo a la alineación para atacar a Corbin Burnes.
Ese ataque llegó de repente en la tercera entrada.
Heliot Ramos empató el partido con su decimotercer jonrón. George Lombard Jr. le siguió más adelante en la entrada con un jonrón de dos carreras, el quinto de la temporada.
El batazo de Lombard recorrió, según las estimaciones de Statcast, 424 pies, el jonrón más largo de su carrera en las Grandes Ligas.
Spencer Jones conectó un jonrón justo después, su undécimo. A continuación, lanzó una bola que se calculó que recorrió 448 pies. Los dos jonrones de los novatos sumaron un total de 872 pies.
Los Yankees habían pasado de ir perdiendo 1-0 a ponerse 4-1 por delante y habían obligado a Burnes a abandonar el partido tras solo 2 2/3 entradas. Parecía el tipo de remontada de los jóvenes que podría sacar adelante a una alineación en la que faltaban los titulares lesionados.
En cambio, esas cuatro carreras fueron toda la producción ofensiva de los Yankees.
Diecinueve outs demuestran lo mucho que ha dado un giro el partido
Cinco relevos de los Diamondbacks sumaron entre todos 6 1/3 entradas sin encajar carreras tras la salida de Burnes. Los Yankees solo consiguieron tres hits contra ese grupo y no anotaron en las últimas 19 eliminaciones.
Justin Martínez lanzó una quinta entrada sin permitir carreras y se llevó la victoria, mejorando su balance a 3-0. Brent Headrick cargó con la derrota, quedando con un balance de 7-4. No se concedió ningún salvamento.
Los Yankees terminaron el día con 216 jonrones, liderando la Liga Americana, pero su poderío no pudo compensar el colapso que vino después.
Warren y Headrick pierden el quinto
Warren llegó a la quinta entrada defendiendo la ventaja de 4-1. Lars Nootbaar conectó un doble, Ketel Marte un sencillo y Gabriel Moreno recibió una base por bolas, llenando las bases con un out. Aaron Boone recurrió a Brent Headrick, uno de los lanzadores del bullpen más utilizados por los Yankees.
Headrick ponchó a Perdomo y luego concedió una base por bolas a Corbin Carroll con las bases llenas, dejando el marcador en 4-2. Arenado mandó una bola rápida justo fuera por la línea del jardín izquierdo antes de conectar con fuerza el siguiente lanzamiento para un grand slam, dando a Arizona una ventaja de 6-4.
Headrick disputaba su 79.ª salida, la segunda cifra más alta de las Grandes Ligas, y, según se informó, la velocidad media de su bola rápida estaba aproximadamente 1,3 mph por debajo de su media de la temporada.
Headrick dijo que el problema era la precisión, no el cansancio.
«Me sentí bien, pero me faltó precisión y me quedé atrás respecto a los bateadores», dijo Headrick.
Warren se fue del partido con cuatro carreras encajadas, seis hits y tres bases por bolas en 4 1/3 entradas. Boone ha dicho que Warren hará una salida más como titular en la temporada regular contra Baltimore antes de pasar al bullpen en octubre.
Warren apoyó al relevo que se hizo cargo de la situación complicada que él había dejado.
«Nos ha dado un montón de problemas todo el año», dijo Warren. «Es un rollo, pero está claro que contamos con él, y nos ha ido muy bien con él todo el año, y va a seguir haciéndolo bien».
Arizona sigue sumando mientras el bullpen de los Yankees flaquea
Perdomo impulsó una carrera con un triple ante John Schreiber en la séptima entrada, y Carroll le siguió con un sencillo impulsor que dejó el marcador final en 8-4. Arizona terminó con siete carreras sin respuesta y se aseguró su 47.ª victoria tras remontada, la mejor marca de la MLB.
Los Yankees también se quedaron sin poder ver a Clarke Schmidt en el bullpen, como tenían previsto. El lanzador diestro tuvo que dejar de calentar por unos calambres cerca del brazo que se le había operado. Las primeras pruebas de fuerza fueron alentadoras, y se esperaba que Schmidt fuera examinado una vez que el equipo volviera a Nueva York.
Por qué esta podría ser la derrota más cara de los Yankees en 2026
Tras dos derrotas seguidas en Arizona, los Yankees vuelven al Yankee Stadium con Tampa Bay en condiciones de zanjar la lucha por el título de la División Este de la Liga Americana en el campo de Nueva York.
El daño va más allá de haber desperdiciado una ventaja. El Tampa Bay llega ahora al Bronx y solo necesita una victoria en la doble jornada del martes para asegurarse el título de la División Este de la Liga Americana, ya que esa victoria también le garantizaría el desempate en la serie de la temporada.
Eso da lugar a la consecuencia más incómoda del colapso de Arizona: los Yankees podrían verse obligados a ver cómo los Rays celebran el título de división en el Yankee Stadium, en el mismo campo donde Nueva York esperaba mantener viva la lucha hasta la última semana.
¿Qué le parece? Deje su comentario a continuación.

Nolan Arenado hit his third grand slam of the season to cap a five-run fifth and the Arizona Diamondbacks kept their slim National League wild card chances alive with an 8-4 victory over the New York Yankees on Sunday in Phoenix.
Geraldo Perdomo had two hits and two RBIs and five Arizona relievers limited the Yankees to three hits in 6 1-3 scoreless innings as the D-backs scored the final seven runs for their major league-leading 47th comeback win.
Heliot Ramos, George Lombard Jr. and Spencer Jones homered for the Yankees, who fell six games behind Tampa Bay in the AL East. The Yankees lead the American League with 216 homers. Lombard had two hits.
Lars Nootbaar and Gabriel Moreno had two hits and scored twice and Ketel Marte had two hits for the Diamondbacks, who have won two straight games.
The D-backs (82-74) remained five games behind NL wild-card leaders Chicago Cubs and San Diego Padres (both 87-69) and four behind the Philadelphia Phillies (86-70) with six to play.
The D-backs would lose a tiebreaker to the Cubs, and tiebreakers against the Padres and Phillies have yet to be determined. The D-backs end the season with three games at Colorado and the final three at San Diego.
Justin Martinez (3-0), the second Arizona reliever to follow Corbin Burnes, struck out two in the fifth for the victory.
The Yankees lost their second straight after winning four of five.
Nootbaar started the D-backs' five-run fifth with a one-out double off Yankees starter Will Warren. Marte singled and Moreno walked to load the bases. Brent Headrick (7-4) entered and struck out Perdomo before walking Corbin Carroll to force in a run.
Arenado followed with his 381-foot homer into the Arizona bullpen for a 6-4 edge. He has five homers in his last 10 games and is tied with Houston's Yordan Alvarez for the major league lead in grand slams.
Perdomo tripled in a run and scored on Carroll's single in a two-run seventh.
The D-backs took a 1-0 lead in the first on singles by Nootbaar, Marte and Perdomo. Warren gave up six hits and four runs in 4 1/3 innings, with three walks and four strikeouts.
Ramos, Lombard and Jones homered four batters apart in a four-run third off Burnes for a 4-1 lead. Ramos homered with two outs before Luis Garcia Jr. singled and Lombard and Jones hit back-to-back shots. Lombard's went an estimated 424 feet. Jones' went 448.Burnes gave up four runs and five hits, with two walks and two strikeouts in 2 2/3 innings. He has given up nine runs and five homers in 10 1-3 innings of three starts since returning after a 15-month absence after Tommy John surgery.

In the final game and rubber match of their three-game road series against the Arizona Diamondbacks (82-74), the Yankees (89-66) coughed up an early lead to lose 8-4.
Here are the takeaways...
-- Will Warren got the nod to start the game, and delivered a solid outing... until the fifth inning. Up to that point, Warren had allowed one earned run - an RBI single in the first inning by Diamondbacks shortstop Geraldo Perdomo - and struck out four batters through four full innings. The Yankees entered the fifth inning leading 4-1 (thanks to home runs from Heliot Ramos, George Lombard Jr., and Spencer Jones), but after Warren surrendered two hits and a walk to load the bases with just one man out, he was pulled in favor of left-handed reliever Brent Headrick.
-- Headrick struck out Perdomo to record the second out, but he couldn't close the door on the frame, issuing a free pass to Corbin Carroll to bring in one run before surrendering a grand slam to Nolan Arenado which gave Arizona a 6-4 lead.
-- Of those five earned runs surrendered in the fifth, three were attributed to Warren, and two to Headrick.
-- New York's right-handed reliever John Schreiber allowed two more runs in the seventh inning, surrendering a triple to Perdomo and a single to Carroll which brought the shortstop home. For Arizona, former Yankee Jonathan Loáisiga recorded the final six outs, facing the minimum six batters without allowing a run to wrap up the 8-4 loss.
Game MVP: Nolan Arenado
Arenado's grand slam flipped the game on its head, and the massive momentum-shifting blast gave the Snakes a lead they wouldn't relinquish.
Highlights
What's next
The Yankees travel back home on Monday and will kick off a pivotal three game series against the AL East divisional leading Tampa Bay Rays on Tuesday at 1:05 p.m.
Of course, now 6.0 games back of Tampa Bay for first place in the AL East with just seven regular season games remaining, the Yankees need a miracle to win the division.
Carlos Rodón (2.95 ERA, 1.13 WHIP in 76.1 IP) is set to take the mound for the Yankees.
The Rays will send out Nick Martinez (2.94 ERA, 1.07 WHIP in 171.1 IP).

The final road game of the 2026 regular season is upon us, as the Yankees will conclude it with a seven-game homestand before likely hosting the Red Sox for the Wild Card Series. If the season ends there, this is the end of the line for the gray uniforms for 2026, but obviously, we all hope we'll see them next in Tampa (and more) in early October.
Looking to end a road slate that has been very generous to the Yankees on a high note is Will Warren, who's finishing his sophomore season strong after his great start to the campaign unraveled into a bit of a mess over the summer. Rotation reinforcements that threatened to throw him in the bullpen never came with the recurring injuries, so he'll finish 2026 with 30 starts for the second straight season. This is No. 29, as he enters with a 3.89 ERA (108 ERA+) and 4.07 FIP in 148 innings. No matter what happens from here, Warren has had a successful year in solidifying himself as a true MLB-caliber rotation arm.
Opposing him will be a former Cy Young winner trying to round into form off Tommy John surgery in Corbin Burnes, whom Yankees fans remember well from his lone season in Baltimore in 2024. Returning from a 16-month absence on September 8 to help with the playoff push, Burnes has allowed five runs across 7.2 innings with six strikeouts to two walks against the Royals and Marlins. He isn't totally built up, having thrown 75 pitches in his last start, so expect him to settle around 80-85 today. He's always befuddled the Yankees, pitching to a 1.93 ERA across 23.1 innings in his career, but he doesn't have a win in any of those four starts.
Ben Rice will once again lead off, followed by Cody Bellinger, Heliot Ramos, and Luis García Jr. We've seen better ABs and swings from George Lombard Jr. lately, who'll bat fifth. Spencer Jones is back after a one-day absence due to a sore foot and will bat in front of Anthony Volpe, Austin Wells, and José Caballero.
Lars Nootbaar will also be a repeat leadoff hitter for the D-backs, followed by Ketel Marte, Gabriel Moreno, and Geraldo Perdomo. Corbin Carroll is batting fifth, Nolan Arenado will bat sixth, and former Blue Jay Jesús Sánchez bats seventh ahead of last night's hero Pavin Smith and Tim Tawa.

D-backs strive to make more 'magic' happen vs. Yankees
(Photo credit: Matt Kartozian)
Arizona manager Torey Lovullo said he felt 'a little bit of magic' in a 5-3 walk-off win over the New York Yankees on Saturday, the night the Diamondbacks celebrated the 25th anniversary of their 2001 World Series title.
The Diamondbacks will take wins however they can get them as they continue an uphill fight for a National League wild-card berth in Sunday afternoon's finale of a three-game series vs. the Yankees in Phoenix.
New York's Will Warren (10-6, 3.89 ERA) will oppose Arizona's Corbin Burnes (0-0, 5.87) in a battle of right-handers.
'There was a ton of energy in the stadium,' said Lovullo, noting that most of the players from the 2001 team were on hand, 'so maybe there was a little bit of magic somewhere in these rafters that everybody picked up on.'
Pavin Smith's two-run, game-winning homer saved the Diamondbacks for a night, but work remains.
'We have to get inside a certain number,' said Lovullo, whose team will finish the regular season next week with a pair of three-game series at Colorado and San Diego. 'We know it, and this team is driving for something they feel they are able to do.'
Arizona (81-74) is five games behind the Chicago Cubs (86-69) and San Diego (86-69) and four behind Philadelphia (85-70) for the NL's three wild-card spots. Each team has seven games remaining.
The Yankees (89-65) fell five games behind first-place Tampa Bay (94-60) in the AL East. Those teams will meet in a four-game series in Yankee Stadium beginning with a split doubleheader on Tuesday and already have clinched a postseason berth.
'I have a ton of confidence in the guys we have rolling out there right now,' New York manager Aaron Boone said after Aaron Judge (calf strain) landed on the 10-day injured list Saturday.
Warren worked the Yankees' playoff clincher Monday at Minnesota, although he did not get a decision after giving up two runs (both unearned) in 5 2/3 innings of an 8-3 win. He struck out six and walked two.
Warren has been a workhorse on a staff that has faced injury issues. He will make his 29th start, second on the team behind Cam Schlittler (32).
'We've got a veteran core that's been here before, and we're looking to do big things,' Warren said of the upcoming postseason.
Warren has faced the Diamondbacks once in his career, giving up two runs on one hit -- a Corbin Carroll two-run homer -- in five innings of a no-decision on April 1, 2025.
Burnes will make his third start since being activated from the injured list Sept. 8 after a 15-month absence following Tommy John surgery. He gave up five runs in 4 2/3 innings but didn't figure into the decision in Monday's 8-7 victory over Miami, striking out four with no walks.
'It's all about cutter command,' Burnes said of his pet pitch, which he traditionally throws about 50% of the time. 'Just have to be more consistent with that,'
Burnes is 0-2 with a 1.93 ERA in four career starts against the Yankees. Paul Goldschmidt is 10-for-34 with a homer against the four-time All-Star and 2021 NL Cy Young Award winner.
--Field Level Media

Nueva York, Nueva York.- Cody Bellinger conectó dos jonrones de dos carreras, impulsó cinco carreras y los Yankees de Nueva York aplastaron a los Reales de Kansas City por 13-4 el sábado por la tarde.
El abridor de Nueva York, Will Warren (2-0), igualó su récord personal con 11 ponches y lanzó un juego de dos carreras en siete entradas.
Bellinger conectó un jonrón de dos carreras durante una entrada de cinco carreras en la tercera entrada contra Noah Cameron (1-1) y llevó a Nueva York a su victoria más abultada de la temporada. Bellinger conectó un jonrón de dos carreras contra Mitch Spence en la sexta entrada, después de haber impulsado una carrera con un sencillo en la cuarta.
Bellinger logró su vigésimo partido con múltiples jonrones de su carrera y los Yankees conectaron cuatro jonrones por segunda vez en la temporada.
Bellinger conectó su primer jonrón entre un batazo de dos carreras de Amed Rosario y un jonrón solitario de Ben Rice, aprovechando los Yankees un error de tres bases del jardinero central Kyle Isbel en un elevado de JC Escarra.
Isbel le arrebató la pelota del guante al jardinero derecho Jac Caglianone cuando ambos se encontraban cerca de la zona de advertencia, y los Yankees respondieron con su demostración de poder contra el lanzador zurdo.
Rosario, abriendo el orden al bate por segunda vez en la temporada, envió un lanzamiento cortado a las gradas del jardín derecho. Tras una base por bolas de Aaron Judge, Bellinger conectó un slider en el primer lanzamiento que llegó al segundo piso del jardín derecho, poniendo el marcador 4-0 a favor de su equipo.
Dos bateadores después, Rice conectó un jonrón por tercer partido consecutivo al mandar la bola rápida de Cameron a las gradas del jardín derecho.
Escarra conectó un doble productor y un triple de dos carreras en la séptima entrada. Rosario también impulsó una carrera con un sencillo antes de que Bellinger volviera a conectar. Randal Grichuk impulsó su primera carrera como Yankee con un elevado de sacrificio en las últimas entradas.
Cameron fue castigado con siete carreras, la mayor cantidad en su carrera (cinco limpias), y siete hits en cuatro entradas.
Carter Jensen conectó un jonrón de dos carreras en la séptima entrada, pero los Royals sufrieron su sexta derrota consecutiva y la novena en 11 partidos. Kansas City también perdió su décimo partido consecutivo contra los Yankees desde el segundo juego de la Serie Divisional de la Liga Americana de 2024.
Antes de que Cameron hiciera su primer lanzamiento, el mánager de los Royals, Matt Quatraro, fue expulsado por el árbitro de segunda base, Nestor Ceja.

item.content:encoded:
PHOENIX — Los Yankees se pasaron casi toda la noche del sábado lidiando con dos realidades en el Chase Field. Cam Schlittler volvió a ofrecerles una gran salida, pero cada entrada cobró más importancia después de que Tampa Bay ya se hubiera llevado la victoria con un tanto decisivo en la última entrada.
Nueva York tuvo la oportunidad de evitar que sus cada vez más remotas opciones en la División Este de la Liga Americana se le escaparan aún más. En cambio, los Yankees se fueron con una derrota por 5-3 ante los Diamondbacks de Arizona, lo que amplió su desventaja en la división a cinco partidos cuando solo quedan ocho por disputar.
Los Yankees hicieron lo suficiente para que el partido se pudiera ganar. Ben Rice conectó un fly de sacrificio en la quinta entrada. Heliot Ramos y Austin Wells conectaron jonrones en la sexta. Schlittler superó su primer bajón serio en el control en semanas y terminó seis entradas concediendo solo una carrera limpia.
Arizona siguió respondiendo. Jordan Lawlar neutralizó la primera ventaja de Nueva York con un triple de dos carreras en la quinta entrada, después de que Schlittler fallara al intentar atrapar un toque. Corbin Carroll empató el partido con un fly de sacrificio en la sexta entrada, tras dos bases por bolas y un sencillo de toque que llenaron las bases.
Lo que estaba en juego ya estaba claro antes del primer lanzamiento. Varios jugadores de los Yankees vieron desde el vestuario de visitantes cómo Tampa Bay vencía a Boston por 2-1, un resultado que situaba a los Rays cinco partidos por delante. Nueva York había ganado ocho de sus últimos diez partidos, pero la racha de Tampa Bay casi no dejaba margen para perder otra oportunidad.
A continuación, los Yankees contaron con dos entradas sin puntos de su bullpen. Brent Headrick consiguió dos outs en la séptima antes de que Paul Blackburn terminara esa entrada y se encargara de la octava. El marcador se mantuvo en 3-3, lo que dejaba a Nueva York a una entrada limpia de tener otra oportunidad al bate.
Schlittler había hecho lo suficiente para mantener a los Yankees en el partido. Cedió tres hits y tres carreras, solo una limpia, y se anotó seis strikeouts en 98 lanzamientos. Su promedio de carreras limpias bajó a 1,94. Para entonces, el margen de error era ya casi nulo.
Fue entonces cuando el partido dio un giro con la decisión más decisiva de Aaron Boone de toda la noche respecto al bullpen.
Boone recurre a Fulmer con el partido en juego
Boone le pasó la parte baja de la novena a Michael Fulmer en lugar de al cerrador David Bednar. Fulmer había lanzado dos tercios de una entrada sin encajar carreras en la victoria del viernes por 9-2, mientras que Bednar no había lanzado desde que hizo dos entradas el miércoles en Minnesota.
Fulmer parecía haber eliminado a Ildemaro Vargas con un strikeout en un lanzamiento con cuenta completa, pero Vargas impugnó la decisión a través del sistema automático de bolas y strikes de la MLB. El lanzamiento se consideró bola, lo que le dio a Arizona una base por bolas para abrir el turno.
Fulmer ponchó a Lawlar. A continuación, Pavin Smith entró como bateador suplente y mandó el segundo lanzamiento de Fulmer, un «cutter», 391 pies al campo derecho para un jonrón de dos carreras que dio la victoria.
Juan Morillo se llevó la victoria para Arizona, mejorando su balance a 5-4. Fulmer sufrió su primera derrota y vio cómo su promedio de carreras limpias subía de 1,59 a 3,09. No hubo salvamento.
La decisión llamó la atención porque Bednar llegaba a la noche con 34 salvamentos y una efectividad de 2,58. Fulmer, fichado por los Yankees a finales de agosto, solo había lanzado 11 1/3 entradas en las Grandes Ligas esta temporada antes del sábado y sigue formando parte de un bullpen muy concurrido de la postemporada.
Schlittler asume la culpa tras una racha irregular
Un error de Schlittler en la quinta entrada ayudó a Arizona a anotar dos veces, y ocho lanzamientos seguidos fuera de la zona al inicio de la sexta propiciaron la remontada que empató el partido. Se recuperó ponchando a Nolan Arenado y a Tim Tawa con dos corredores en posición de anotar.
El lanzador diestro se centró en su propio error tras el partido.
«Asumo toda la culpa por eso», dijo Schlittler. «Cometí un error ahí y dejé que nos marcaran dos carreras. Así es el béisbol, pero esa la tengo yo».
Schlittler ha cedido una carrera limpia o menos en 24 salidas como titular, lo que le convierte, junto a Sandy Koufax y Bob Gibson, en uno de los únicos lanzadores de la Era de la Bola Viva con al menos 24 salidas de este tipo en una temporada, sin contar los «openers».
El descanso de Bednar acentúa el contraste en el bullpen
La secuencia de relevos de los Yankees ofreció un anticipo de la postemporada. Headrick y Blackburn sumaron entre ambos dos entradas sin encajar carreras antes de la novena. Bednar no llegó a salir, mientras que Fulmer lanzó dos días seguidos.
Fulmer llegaba al sábado con una ERA de 1,59 y había limitado a sus rivales a un promedio de bateo de 0,171 en sus apariciones con los Yankees. La diferencia en la carga de trabajo era aún más marcada: Fulmer había lanzado el viernes, mientras que Bednar había tenido dos días completos de descanso tras su salida de dos entradas del miércoles.
Esto es importante ahora que los Yankees están reorganizando una plantilla de lanzadores que se reducirá de cara a octubre. Bednar es una opción consolidada para las últimas entradas. Fulmer ha lanzado lo suficientemente bien como para seguir en la pugna por un puesto en la plantilla, pero su puesto está menos asegurado, ya que varios relevistas compiten por las limitadas plazas de la postemporada.
El sábado supuso otro momento de evaluación, y esta vez se dio en un momento de máxima presión.
Los Yankees pierden más terreno antes del enfrentamiento con los Rays
Con esta derrota, los Yankees se quedan con un balance de 89-65. Tampa Bay sube a 94-60, lo que deja a Nueva York a cinco partidos de distancia en la División Este de la Liga Americana. Los Yankees siguen teniendo una ventaja de 5 partidos y medio sobre Boston en la lucha por el primer puesto de comodín de la Liga Americana.
Boone reconoció lo estrecho que se ha vuelto el camino con cuatro partidos contra Tampa Bay a partir del martes en el Yankee Stadium.
«Si les barreríamos, entonces la cosa se pondría interesante», dijo Boone. «Pero no puedes barrerlos antes del partido [del domingo]».
Los Yankees cierran la serie contra Arizona el domingo, con Will Warren como lanzador previsto para enfrentarse a Corbin Burnes. Tras el partido del sábado, Nueva York debe mantener viva la lucha por el título de división y, al mismo tiempo, decidir en qué relevos confía Boone cuando llegue la próxima novena entrada empatada.

By DAVID BRANDT
PHOENIX (AP) — Pavin Smith hit a two-run homer in the ninth inning to lift the Arizona Diamondbacks over the New York Yankees 5-3 on Saturday night, giving the D-backs’ slim playoff hopes a boost.
Ildemaro Vargas started the ninth with a walk, winning an ABS challenge on a full-count pitch initially called a strike. After Jordan Lawlar struck out, Smith pinch hit and drove a cutter from Michael Fulmer (0-1) into the right-field seats.
Arizona pulled within four games of Philadelphia for the final NL wild card with seven games remaining, snapping a three-game losing streak on a night the franchise celebrated the 25th anniversary of its 2001 World Series win over the Yankees.
Juan Morillo (1-1) pitched 1 1/3 hitless innings. D-backs right-hander Brandon Pfaadt gave up one run on four hits and a walk over 4 1/3 innings, striking out three.
New York’s 11 walk-off losses are one behind San Francisco, which has the most in the major leagues.
New York ace Cam Schlittler gave up three runs — but only one earned — over six innings. The right-hander allowed three hits and three walks, striking out six and lowering his ERA to 1.94.
Schlitter’s 24 starts with one or no earned runs this year is one shy of the record in the live-ball era since 1920, set by Sandy Koufax in 1963, according to Major League Baseball.
The All-Star didn’t allow a hit until the fifth inning when Nolan Arenado lined a one-out single into left field. The right-hander then made a costly error on Tim Tawa’s sacrifice bunt attempt, dropping the ball as he tried to throw to first. Jordan Lawlar capitalized on the miscue with a two-out triple into the left-center field gap for a 2-1 lead.
Austin Wells and Heliot Ramos hit solo homers off Kevin Ginkel in the sixth to push the Yankees ahead 3-2.
Corbin Carroll hit a sacrifice fly in the bottom half but Schlittler limited damage by striking out Arenado and Tawa to end the threat.

The New York Yankees suffered a tough loss on Saturday night, falling to the Arizona Diamondbacks 5-3 on Pavin Smith’s two-run walk-off home run in the ninth inning.
The loss came after the Yankees twice held a lead earlier in the game. New York broke through in the fifth inning when Austin Wells, Anthony Volpe and José Caballero opened the frame with consecutive singles to load the bases. Ben Rice followed with a sacrifice fly that brought home Wells and put the Yankees ahead 1-0.
Arizona answered in the bottom half of the inning, taking a 2-1 lead on Jordan Lawler’s two-run triple. Both runs were unearned against Yankees starter Cam Schlittler, who committed a fielding error on a sacrifice bunt during the inning.
New York responded quickly in the sixth. Heliot Ramos tied the game with a solo home run before Wells put the Yankees back in front with his 13th home run of the season. Both home runs came against Arizona reliever Kevin Ginkel.
Schlittler ran into trouble again in the bottom of the sixth after issuing two walks and allowing a single to load the bases with nobody out. Corbin Carroll tied the game with a sacrifice fly, but Schlittler struck out the next two batters to escape further damage.
Schlittler completed six innings, allowing three runs on three hits with three walks and six strikeouts over 98 pitches. Only one of the three runs was earned, and his season earned-run average dropped to 1.94.
Neither team scored again until the ninth, when Smith ended the game with his two-run homer off Michael Fulmer.
The Yankees will finish the series Sunday at 4:10 p.m. Will Warren will face Corbin Burnes.

item.content:encoded:
One would figure that with Cam Schlittler going on Saturday night, this would be the game for the Yankees to win if they had any hope for a last-ditch AL East comeback, but something about Arizona wore down the likely Cy Young Award winner tonight. The Snakes were pesky, annoying, and other terms my editors won’t let me use while in the batter’s box tonight, finally breaking through on a Pavin Smith walk-off home run, to win it, 5-3.
Right off the top, I need to be grumpy about something. Nobody likes West Coast games and nobody likes the fact that every time the Yankees are on the West Coast, they play more night games than day games. This goes double for West Coast Yankee fans, because the beautiful thing about cheering for an East Coast team is they start playing when you get off work, or when you’re just finishing your Saturday morning coffee, the game takes three hours and you have the evening to yourself. That doesn’t happen on these trips.
Now, the Diamondbacks were celebrating the only World Series title in history, 25 years ago this season. I get it, you want to have a special event, the team isn’t very good so the end of the season starts to drag a little bit, you want a little spice. I even respect the cheek of waiting until the Yankees are in town. What I don’t respect is being completely incapable of running a functioning ceremony. The Yankees have Old Timer’s Day every year, they designate a special start time and at that time, the festivities have concluded and we can get down to the reason we’re all here, to watch a baseball game, which I don’t think is an unreasonable expectation at a baseball stadium with a baseball team in town.
The Diamondbacks started their pregame ceremonies at 4:30pm local time, with a scheduled 5:10pm first pitch. They absolutely blew past that in a way that, in my opinion, was both unprofessional and downright insulting. The four clocks I have ready access to in my apartment agreed: Brandon Pfaadt didn’t throw his first offering to Ben Rice until 5:42pm. This was an absolute joke of a start to the series’ second game. That all this happened in a city I’m predisposed to dislike already was…whatever the anti-cherry on top. I also firmly don’t like the existence of Phoenix as a city in general so I was always going to be ticked off watching this one.
I said in the gamethread that we had maybe begun to develop outsized expectations for Cam Schlittler. He’s been SO good, for long enough, that we needed to remember the other team all drives nice cars and lives in nice houses too. While Cam did get through 4.1 innings without allowing a hit, the Diamondbacks pushed a pair of runs across in the fifth. Nolan Arenado reached with a one-out single, before Tim Tawa attempted to give himself up with a sac bunt. Schlittler couldn’t corral what should have been an out though, an error that put two men on, and #9 hitter Jordan Lawlar made him pay:
Funny enough, because Schlittler was charged with that error, both of the runs were unearned, and he still hasn’t allowed more than a single earned run in eight starts now. The Yankees would tie the game the next inning, but all those extra pitches taxed his right arm, and I think had a major impact on what would happen in the sixth.
Speaking of tying the game, Heliot Ramos was brought to New York because of his opposite field power. He stunk in his first taste of East Coast baseball, but has looked much more representative in his last 20 games, and flexed that oppo pop within moments of Schlittler getting back in the dugout:
Corbin Carroll ran down a sinking Anthony Volpe liner for the second out, a very nice play that loomed larger when Austin Wells stepped to the plate:
Wells is getting hot at the right time, with three home runs in his last five games and he’s actually been a league average hitter since August 1! The nice thing about being a good defensive catcher is if you can just not embarrass yourself at the plate, you’re a major asset for your team.
The good vibes only lasted until Cam got back on the mound though. I think the error and the triple shook him up a little, and we’ve seen this happen before. Schlittler’s a high-energy guy, when that energy is less than positive I do think he gets a little in his own head and starts to overthrow. He walked the first two batters of the inning on eight total pitches, completely uncompetitive at-bats that are just so out of whack with what he’s done so far this season.
A soft Geraldo Perdomo bunt loaded the bases, and Cam did seem to lock in at that point. Corbin Carroll did bring in the third Snakes run of the game — and the only earned for Cam — but the ace got both Arenado and Tawa to whiff to end the threat. It was a weird one for Schlittler tonight, but 6.0 IP and one earned run is what the line reads.
The bullpen wasn’t exactly dynamite in Cam’s stead; the Diamondbacks have the third-lowest strikeout rate in baseball and their ability to grind out at-bats showed, even if the Yankees got through eight innings keeping the game tied at three. This was a long, miserable game, and wasn’t helped by the fact the Yankees couldn’t really find the nine-run spark that they showed on Friday.
If nothing else, I got to re-hate Michael Fulmer, and all those feelings from 2016 sprung forth anew. He walked the leadoff batter to open the ninth, and gave up the walk-off dinger to Pavin Smith:

Yankees at Diamondbacks. Cam Schlittler dominating in early innings
The Yankees broke through with the first run of the game in the top of the fifth inning, while the Diamondbacks are still looking for their first hit off Yankees right-hander Cam Schlittler.
The Diamondbacks trail the Yankees, 1-0, after 4½ innings as play continued at Chase Field on Saturday, Sept. 19.
The Yankees loaded the bases on three singles in the fifth off right-hander Brandon Pfaadt, prompting manager Torey Lovullo to make an aggressive move to his bullpen. Right-hander Justin Martinez entered and recorded two fly-ball outs, the first of which, by Ben Rice, was deep enough to score the first run of the night.
The Diamondbacks are trying to keep their slim playoff hopes alive with a win. Meanwhile, the San Diego Padres, whom the Diamondbacks are hoping to catch, were losing to the Marlins at Petco Park.
The game started about a half-hour late after a lengthy pregame ceremony honoring the Diamondbacks’ 2001 World Series team.
With former radio voice Greg Schulte hosting the ceremony, the Diamondbacks introduced players, coaches and staff from the ‘01 team. Randy Johnson was the last one announced. While everyone else entered the field from beyond the right-field fence, Johnson came out of the home bullpen in left field, a call back to his relief appearance in Game 7 of the World Series.
One of the memorable moments of the pregame ceremony was when trumpeter Dr. Jesse McGuire, performing the national anthem as he did at the World Series in 2001, hit a sour note on his instrument. Then the trumpet gave out completely, and McGuire acted quickly by grabbing the microphone and singing the rest of the Star-Spangled Banner.
Afterward, he received a hug from Diamondbacks manager Torey Lovullo as the crowd cheered.
—Nick Piercoro and Jose M. Romero
With his team teetering on the brink of elimination, Lovullo’s job status is again a topic of discussion. Lovullo understands. For him, it’s nothing new.
“It seems to be a very important part of the conversation for a lot of people,” Lovullo said on Saturday, Sept. 19, a day after his team lost for the third consecutive day to drop five games out of a playoff spot with eight games remaining.
“For me, it’s real, I understand it, but it’s the realities of this game. You’ve got to win. That’s what it comes down to. Have we won enough? You know, I want to win every game that we play.”
Lovullo, in his 10th season as Diamondbacks manager, has worked as a “lame-duck” manager in four of the past six seasons. He seemed to reference that history, as well as the fact that he had to “fight for everything” during his playing career.
But he said that, for now, at least, he remains focused on doing what he can to help his players and coaches finish out the season.
“When it’s time to worry about it or think about it, whether that’s sooner than later, I will,” he said. “I’ve got to do my job. If I'm worried about different things that I can’t control, then I'm not doing my job for that group in there. I’m doing fine. I’m doing fine. Because I've lived in this space for a long time. I understand the playbook. I understand the realities of this game.”
Last year, Lovullo went into the final weekend of the year with similar questions surrounding him. He found out a day after the season ended that he would be coming back for another year.
The situation is believed to be similar to then: Lovullo has strong support from the baseball operations department and general manager Mike Hazen, but how he is viewed by ownership is less certain.
Lovullo has two postseason appearances — 2017 and 2023 — during his managerial tenure, but he also has presided over multiple late-season collapses. If this year's team continues to stumble, it would mark a third consecutive year the Diamondbacks fell short in September.
Hazen is working under the five-year extension he signed in September 2023. His deal runs through 2028.
The Diamondbacks entered Saturday, Sept. 19, facing long odds at a postseason berth. FanGraphs put their chances at claiming a wild-card spot at about 5%.
—Nick Piecoro
Justin Martinez leaves impression on manager
Members of the 2001 Diamondbacks World Series team milled about in front of the home dugout at Chase Field on Friday, Sept. 18, catching up, taking photos and conducting interviews.
Justin Martinez walked among them, asking each one he approached to sign a baseball. The Diamondbacks reliever later put the ball in a case he had with him in the team clubhouse.
Lovullo said Martinez seeking autographs of veterans is a throwback to a previous generation of players.
“I love it,” Lovullo said. “There was probably seven fistfights between those teammates, firstfights don’t happen anymore. It’s just a different level of camaraderie. But players care about the same thing, and that’s to win the world championship.
“So ‘J-Mart’ was probably just getting a feel for the common denominator based on what drove that team, and that’s a brotherhood that you can’t replace.”
Lovullo added that he's happy that the current team has players that are fans of baseball on that level.
“That he gets to touch their emotions makes it even better. That’s vintage J-Mart," Lovullo said.
— José M. Romero
Yankees at Diamondbacks, 5:10 p.m., Cox, Ch. 34
Diamondbacks RHP Brandon Pfaadt (7-3, 3.77) vs. Yankees RHP Cam Schlittler (14-6, 1.95).
At Chase Field: Pfaadt gave up six runs in 6⅔ innings against the Rangers in his most recent start. All six runs came in the fifth inning, in which Pfaadt was ruled to have missed the bag while covering first, opening the door for the final four runs of the inning to score. … Pfaadt has had a strong past few months overall, but his past five starts have been rough. He has posted a 5.74 ERA in 31⅓ innings in that stretch. … He has faced the Yankees only once in his career, giving up six runs (five earned) in 4⅓ innings in a game in 2023. … Schlittler looks like the favorite to win the American League Cy Young Award. He has the lowest ERA and WHIP and has logged 184⅔. … He has never faced the Diamondbacks. … Schlittler averages 98 mph with his four-seam fastball. He primarily throws that, his sinker and cutter, only occasionally sprinkling in curveballs and a rare slider.
Coming up
Sunday, Sept. 20: At Chase Field, 1:10 p.m., Diamondbacks RHP Corbin Burnes (0-0, 5.87) vs. Yankees RHP Will Warren (10-6, 3.89).

New York will begin a three-game road series against the Arizona Diamondbacks on Friday.

Although Volpe has been playing better, he isn't guaranteed a spot on the Yankees playoff roster.

C: Austin Wells, Ali Sánchez

New York Right Now
The Yankees have clinched a playoff spot as New York will be hosting a Wild Card series again.

If there's one reason to think the New York Yankees have a minuscule chance of overcoming a five-game deficit in the American League East, it's the probable pitchers every series. Aaron Boone's Bombers can feature one of his many frontline starters on a given night, and in this series against the Arizona Diamondbacks, two of his four best pitchers take the mound.
On paper, you see the first two starters and think the advantage should go to the Yankees, but one issue in particular has hampered their former Cy Young winner. If this team is going to make any noise in the postseason, he'll have to work on it, and it starts with this series.
Friday, Sept. 18 (9:40 p.m. ET): Gerrit Cole (NYY) vs. Eduardo Rodriguez (ARI)
Eduardo Rodriguez has proven to be a playoff-caliber pitcher, and his 2.62 ERA in 178.1 IP is frontline stuff. He is the type of high-level arm they'll see in the postseason. Rodriguez typically pitches to contact, holding opposing batters to an 87.3 MPH average exit velocity and a 33% hard-hit rate. This can be one of those games where the Yankees hit ground balls against him for 7+ innings.
Cole, meanwhile, has been snakebit by the long ball, and it isn't so wild to say that the advantage could go to Rodriguez in this one if Cole pitches the way he has. It's been a concerning turn of events ever since that game against the San Diego Padres. For now, the advantage goes to Rodriguez, who'll want to harken back to his Boston days and shut down the Yankees.
Saturday, Sept. 19 (8:10 p.m. ET): Cam Schlittler (NYY) vs. Brandon Pfadt (ARI)
Pfaadt, though, isn't a slouch by any means, and if the Yankees are going to be without Aaron Judge — which usually means the offense will be listless — what can be said about Rodriguez applies to Pfaadt here.
The 27-year-old Arizona starter has a 68th-percentile groundball rate and holds hitters to a 35.5% hard-hit rate. It could be another instance of the Yankees hitting a ton of ground balls. Most competent offenses should be able to hold their own, but it's hard to trust the Yankees 1-through-9 these days. They might need a great pitching performance by Schlittler and win one of those 2-0 or 3-0 games here.
Pfaadt has one of the best walk rates in baseball. His 5.7% BB% is in the 91st percentile, so he'll force them to make contact, and that can be a recipe for disaster for a team that can't put together runs.
Sunday, Sept. 20 (4:10 p.m. ET): Will Warren (NYY) vs. Corbin Burnes (ARI)
Corbin Burnes has pitched all of 7.2 innings this season. He's coming back from Tommy John surgery, which he had last June. It feels like a quick recovery, and he'll likely be on a pitch limit. That said, the sooner the Yankees can get him back in the game, the better.
Every Warren start can't be a high-scoring affair because he can be brilliant or a disaster, so hopefully they get a brilliant Warren here while also chasing Burnes out of the game quickly. If he's out by the third, they can ground down that bullpen.
Warren is coming off a solid outing against the Twins earlier this week, where he allowed five hits, two runs (zero earned), two walks, and racked up six strikeouts in 5.2 innings.
The advantage should go to the Yankees if Warren gives them length, but again, as with any game, it will come down to whether they can score.

Some New York Yankees fans had been wondering if the team would start to limit Cam Schlittler’s innings or even potentially skip one of his remaining starts with the playoffs in view, but it doesn’t appear that the Yankees are planning on that. At least for now.
The Yankees have locked in their starting pitchers for this weekend’s three-game series in Arizona, and the headline assignment is Schlittler taking the ball Saturday against the Diamondbacks, via MLB.com.
With the club already in the postseason but still chasing both the American League East title and the top Wild Card seed, every start carries extra weight.
Manager Aaron Boone’s staff listed Gerrit Cole for Friday, Schlittler for Saturday, and Will Warren for Sunday, setting up a rotation that showcases the team’s depth heading into the final stretch.
Schlittler’s outing is the one that stands out. The right-hander has been the anchor of New York’s staff all year, posting a 14-6 record with a 1.95 ERA and 228 strikeouts.
Those numbers have made him the clear favorite for the American League Cy Young Award and, in the view of many around the league, the best pitcher in baseball this season … although he has already racked up 184.2 innings. He will face Arizona’s Brandon Pfaadt, who enters with a 7-3 mark and a 3.77 ERA.
The contrast is sharp: a dominant, high-strikeout ace against a solid but far less overwhelming counterpart.
The Yankees’ pitching staff as a whole has been exceptional. Their 3.19 team ERA ranks first in the majors, and they lead the league in fewest earned runs and runs allowed.
They have done it despite injuries that forced constant adjustments. Schlittler’s consistency has allowed Boone to manage the rest of the rotation with an eye toward October.
After this series, the club expects to have Max Fried and Carlos Rodón lined up for Tuesday’s doubleheader against the Tampa Bay Rays, with Cole and Schlittler available later in that set.
Sunday’s starter, Will Warren, has quietly put together a strong campaign of his own (10-6, 3.89 ERA). How Boone uses him in the postseason—whether as a fifth starter or a high-leverage reliever—will be one of the more interesting decisions of the coming weeks.
For now, the immediate focus is this weekend in the desert. Friday’s matchup pits Cole against Eduardo Rodriguez, Sunday features Warren opposite Corbin Burnes, and Saturday belongs to Schlittler.
The Yankees know the Diamondbacks can be dangerous at home, but they also know they possess one of the strongest rotations in the sport.
Giving the ball to Schlittler on Saturday is both a statement of confidence and a practical move. It also demonstrates that New York is not concerned about his workload.
If he continues to pitch the way he has all season, the Yanks will take another step toward securing home-field advantage and heading into October with its best possible alignment. The series begins Friday night. All eyes will be on Saturday.

It wasn't all bad news from a discouraging and frustrating 13-inning defeat at the hands of the Minnesota Twins on Wednesday afternoon, even if it really, really stung for a number of reasons.
The ray of sunshine in what was a rough day for the Yankees' divisional hopes was the return of someone they view as crucial to their chances at a deep playoff run. After a 440-day absence due to Tommy John surgery, Clarke Schmidt made his Yankees return, tossing two-thirds of an inning in the seventh before being removed due to pitch count.
It wasn't the cleanest outing, as he wasn't able to get through a full inning after throwing 24 pitches to four batters, but for someone on a big league mound for the first time in 14 months, you had to like what you saw, striking out a pair and only surrendering a pair of soft-hit singles.
The runway is rather short for the remainder of the season with just 10 games left, but Schmidt will likely see his way into four or so games down the stretch. That gives him a total of five outings to truly figure out where he can fit into a wide-open bullpen trust tree.
Clarke Schmidt's bullpen experience
Converting a full-time starter to the bullpen is not always as easy as it seems, but it's a transition the Yankees will have to make three times as we head into the postseason, with Ryan Weathers' likely return and Will Warren's place in the rotation. That said, Schmidt has a bit of an advantage.
Before becoming a full-time starter at the major-league level in 2023, Schmidt was used almost exclusively as a reliever in his brief big-league stints, most notably in 2022, when he posted a 3.12 ERA in 57.2 innings as part of a makeshift bullpen that got very good results. He didn't get himself high up the totem pole, but he pitched some important innings for the club.
His playoff experience as a reliever was unfortunately one to forget. He was saddled with a pair of losses, first in Game 3 of the ALDS after a squeaker by Oscar Gonzalez got through the infield for a walk-off single, and the second in Game 1 of the ALCS against the Houston Astros, where he allowed home runs to Yuli Gurriel and Chas McCormick in the sixth inning of what would be the start of a sweep.
He was supposed to be in the bullpen the following season, but a mountain of injuries forced him to step up in the rotation, starting what became a nightmarish 2023 season. Since then, Schmidt has made 63 appearances through his season-ending elbow surgery in 2025, all but one as a starter.
That's not in the cards for 2026, so what can he do to be useful for the Yankees in the playoffs?
Where Schmidt could fit into unstable bullpen
Schmidt adds a multi-inning righty option to a bullpen that has a lot of moving parts. He leaned hard on a cutter-slider combo on Wednesday, but also featured his sinker, four-seamer, and curveball. His velocity looked as firm as ever, something that could be enhanced but didn't need to hold back for 100 pitches.
The bullpen's premier multi-inning righty is Paul Blackburn, who relies on a ton of spin and movement in his profile, making him more volatile in games with shoddy command. He, along with closer David Bednar and lefty Brent Headrick, makes up the team's three highest-leverage arms, but it's wide open beneath them, particularly after Fernando Cruz's elbow injury.
John Schreiber has been effective as a righty specialist in a small sample, so he feels like the leader in the clubhouse as the team's sixth-inning arm, but he might not be playable in certain matchups due to his struggles against lefties. Tim Hill's overall struggles, even if he remains sharp against lefties, will also give pause. Michael Fulmer and Luis Gil haven't pitched enough to earn trust in leverage.
There are two ways that Schmidt can be deployed. One of which is as the team's right-handed bridge reliever, as sort of a "platoon" with Ryan Yarbrough (or Weathers, when he returns). Lineups with more right-handed hitters will fare significantly better against Weathers or Yarbrough if the team needs them to come into a big spot to provide some length to the back-end guys, so having a guy with the opposite hand who can fill that role is valuable.
But that role could be reserved for Warren, who's more stretched out than Schmidt and isn't at risk of being removed due to a long inning. I doubt Schmidt would be permitted to throw much more than 30 pitches in a game. That could lead the 30-year-old to be more in the Schreiber role as the sixth-inning guy, possibly pitching in higher leverage if needed due to overuse.
There are a lot of questions about Schmidt as we come down the stretch, but the important thing is that he's back and he's healthy. The more bullpen depth, the merrier.

The Yankees squandered a chance to sweep the Twins Wednesday, dropping a 13-inning gut punch that diminished their chances of catching up to the Rays in the AL East. They’ll head to Phoenix this weekend for a three-game set against the Diamondbacks, who’ve dropped consecutive series and are hanging by a thread in the NL Wild Card race. With a four-game set against the Rays looming next week, this series against Arizona will be crucial in determining if the Yankees control their own destiny heading into the season’s final week. Let’s take a look at the likely starting pitching matchups.
Friday: Gerrit Cole vs. Eduardo Rodriguez (9:40 pm ET)
Tonight at Chase Field, all eyes will be on Gerrit Cole. Aside from the importance of the game on its own merits, it will be a crucial opportunity for the longtime Yankees ace to show whether he can still be counted upon as a frontline starter this postseason. After posting an exemplary 3.11 ERA in his first 16 starts back from Tommy John surgery, he’s stumbled in his last four, allowing 15 runs in 22.2 innings. Most concerning has been his battle with the long ball, having allowed seven in his last two starts. With Cam Schlittler, Max Fried, and Carlos Rodón firing on all cylinders, a strong outing tonight will help reassure the Yankees that Cole’s recent struggles are just a blip and that he belongs squarely in their playoff rotation.
Cole will face a fellow veteran hurler who’s in the midst of a career year. At the age of 33, Eduardo Rodríguez made his first All-Star team this year and has been a rock for the D-Backs, going 15-6 with a 2.62 ERA that quietly ranks fourth in the NL. Opponents are hitting below the Mendoza line against his heater and are slugging just .335 against his changeup, his top complementary pitch. The latter weapon has been particularly effective against righties, against whom the southpaw has fared batter this year than his fellow lefties. Rodríguez labored his last time out, allowing six runs in 5.1 innings, though only three were earned as the D-Backs committed two costly errors in the fifth.
Saturday: Cam Schlittler vs. Brandon Pfaadt (8:10 pm ET)
When the conversation turns from Cy Young to MVP, you’ve entered rarified air. If the season ended today, Cam Schlittler’s 2026 would rank second in Yankees history in WHIP (0.904) and eighth in ERA (1.95). He’s already seventh in strikeouts (228) and could easily crack the top three with two more representative outings. The last time Schlittler allowed more than a run in one of his starts was on August 3rd. He allowed no runs and one hit in his last outing as he ran roughshod over the Mets. At this point in the season, Schlittler is as close to a sure thing as it gets.
He’s lined up to face Brandon Pfaadt. A hero of the D-Backs’ run to the World Series in 2023, Pfaadt has struggled to establish himself in the intervening years. After spending some time in the bullpen and in the minors this year, he rejoined the rotation on June 30 and has been lights out ever since, going 7-2 with a 2.83 ERA over 12 starts. That ERA was as low as 2.38 before his last outing, a six-run implosion in which he allowed 10 hits to the Rangers in 6.1 innings. Pfaadt doesn’t get many strikeouts but also walks few, relying on soft contact generated by his six-pitch mix to work through lineups.
Thursday: Will Warren vs. Corbin Burnes (4:10 pm ET)
Will Warren may have nine lives. In mid-August, it looked like his days in the rotation were numbered with Rodón scheduled to return from injury. Instead, with Fried and Ryan Weathers landing on the shelf, the 27-year-old got a reprieve. He’s made the most of it, going 2-0 with a 1.38 ERA in his last five outings (four starts) while allowing just two home runs. While he’s unlikely to crack the playoff rotation barring injury, Warren has helped reassert himself as a valuable asset in the bullpen this postseason and in the rotation going forward.
The D-Backs are scheduled to hand the ball to Corbin Burnes. After signing a six-year megadeal with Arizona before the 2025 season, he made only 11 starts before missing a year-plus to Tommy John surgery. Burnes has made just two outings since his return and has looked rusty. His last time out, the former Cy Young Award winner allowed five runs in 4.2 innings to the Marlins. He threw just 75 pitches in that start as he continues to ramp up, and it’s unclear if he’ll be permitted to shoulder a full starter’s workload this time out.

On the offensive front, the New York Yankees have a lot to worry about. Pitching-wise, things are okay — more than okay, actually.
Despite a lackluster trade deadline in which general manager Brian Cashman failed to add any relievers, the team bolstered its pitching depth in the weeks that followed. They lucked out by adding John Schreiber, which was essentially a salary dump for the Kansas City Royals, and Clarke Schmidt coming off the IL is another positive.
The Yankees' 5-4 loss to the Minnesota Twins on Wednesday afternoon was an ugly one they needed, and Minnesota's walk-off left a bad taste, while Aaron Judge had another injury scare. But it was another stellar day for the pen, outside of David Bednar letting up two leads in extras. Schmidt is one reason to look forward to what the pen could be in October, and even if he has a little more rust to knock off, there are a few things to be excited about.
Giving length
Schmidt isn't built up, but he should be good to give a little more than an inning at a time as a reliever. While he only pitched 2/3 innings in his return to the mound, it's clear the Yankees are building Schmidt up to go multiple innings. In three of his five rehab starts, he pitched more than one inning. In two of them, he pitched two innings.
Paul Blackburn and Brent Headrick have clearly been overworked. Somebody like Schmidt lightens their load, and soon another starter, Ryan Weathers, will join the bullpen.
More strikeout stuff in the bullpen
The Yankees have desperately needed strikeout stuff, especially in the middle innings. The Yankees have guys who can generate whiffs in Bednar, Blackburn, and Headrick, but that's missing if a starter comes out early. Schmidt gives them that. He struck out two batters in his debut, and despite allowing two hits, he navigated through it because of the whiffs.
Schmidt also showed strikeout stuff in his rehab start. He struck out 11 batters in seven innings. He hasn't had a full season since 2023, but in 2024 and 2025 combined, the veteran hurler had a 9.11 K/9. That should play in October.
No more sweeper?
The sweeper was Schmidt's second-most-used pitch in 2024. It was his third-most-used pitch in 2023. Against the Minnesota Twins, he didn't throw it once. It could be a pitch he's throwing away.
It would be a surprise if he did that, though. Batters hit .210 off it and struck out 33.8% of the time against it in 2024. In 2025, they hit .125 off the sweeper. They struck out 35.8% of the time against it. It's something to look to in future outings.
Potential trade bait
You can never have too much pitching, and if there is one thing the 2026 Yankees understand full well, it's that pitching depth is paramount. It's how they navigated the season.
That said, Schmidt has one year left after this season. The Yankees may want to sell high on him if they don't plan on bringing him back. The rotation should be full again next year, and if they need pitching depth, they have Ryan Weathers and Will Warren.
This season could be a showcase of sorts for Schmidt. The veteran showing he can finish out the season could be a selling point in the winter.
Chances are, Schmidt won't be able to start next year anyway, and if he does, he won't have a full workload since he needs to build back up. The last time he pitched more than 150 innings was in 2023. That said, the Yankees could use this as an opportunity to deal an oft-injured pitcher and fill another area of need.

For their sake, the New York Yankees better hope that superstar outfielder Aaron Judge’s newest injury is only a minor setback.
Judge left Wednesday’s extra-inning loss to the Twins with lower leg tightness, immediately raising concerns among fans that he’ll miss the Yankees’ first playoff series. New York entered play on Sept. 17 in firm control of the AL’s top Wild Card seed, putting them on track to host the No. 5 Red Sox in the first round.
If Judge can’t go when the playoffs begin on Sept. 29, then he won’t be the only notable contributor not in uniform during the Wild Card Series. Each team gets 26 players for their playoff rosters, but no more than 13 pitchers. Some clubs opt for 14 position players and 12 pitchers, though we personally prefer a 13-and-13 balance. Additionally, teams can adjust their rosters between series, and obviously they can replace an injured player if needed.
For this list, we’re only including players who are healthy and active as of Sept. 17. In other words, that means Trent Grisham, Giancarlo Stanton, and Ryan Weathers are among those who didn’t qualify. We’ve also omitted Judge because the Yankees haven’t announced the severity of his left leg injury.
Jasson Domínguez, OF
The writing has long been on the wall for Domínguez, who was recently demoted to Triple-A amid another disappointing season. Even if Judge potentially misses the Wild Card Round, it’s difficult to envision the 23-year-old Domínguez returning as a backup outfielder.
Frankly, the entire situation is unfortunate, because neither Domínguez’s talent nor his work ethic has been the issue. He’s always earned rave reviews for his maturity and overall attitude, but injuries — most notably to his elbow and shoulder — have seemingly sapped him of his once-potent power stroke.
Luis Gil, P
Gil has had an odd career, winning AL Rookie of the Year in 2024 despite debuting three years earlier. Injuries have limited him to a 3.92 ERA over 80.1 innings since the start of 2025, and he recently moved to the bullpen. We’ll see whether the Yankees view the 28-year-old as a long-term reliever, or if they’d bring him to spring training as a starter.
But for now, Gil is on the roster bubble, and we don’t expect him to crack the 26-man playoff squad. Clarke Schmidt’s return gives the Yankees another depth arm, and Gil hasn’t shown that he’s worth carrying on a limited staff. That said, we imagine he’d be among the first names called if injuries strike his teammates.
Paul Goldschmidt, 1B/DH
Goldschmidt turned 39 last week, and it’s unclear whether he’s in the final weeks of a likely Hall of Fame career. He’s totaled 65.3 bWAR, and the majority of the 142 players above him are already in the Hall of Fame or will be when they’re eligible.
Let’s get back to the present. Goldschmidt is hitting just .239 with a .680 OPS in 103 second-half plate appearances, and he’s only capable of playing first or DHing. Ben Rice fills both roles, and Cody Bellinger can also play first if needed.
The one thing potentially working in Goldschmidt’s favor is his .313 average and 1.006 OPS against lefties, but that’s not enough to warrant a roster spot in our eyes. Sorry, Goldy. At least you’d finally earn a World Series ring if the Yankees finish the job.
Will Warren, SP
This might come as a surprise, given that we included Warren in our most recent playoff roster projection. But the more that we think about things, Schmidt’s return feels like a significant blow to Warren’s chances of pitching in October. Do the Yankees really need two long relievers capable of eating up innings if the starter leaves early?
We initially had veteran swingman Ryan Yarbrough in this spot, though he might have the advantage as a left-handed reliever.. He also has a 2.91 ERA in 21.2 second-half innings and has since recovered from a lingering right oblique problem.

While it has been a fairly decent year for New York Yankees rookie OF Spencer Jones, an uncharacteristic performance in Wednesday's series finale against the Minnesota Twins at Target Field has put the 25-year-old under the scanner, with multiple fans sharing their concerns and criticizing him on social media.
Jones went 0-for-6 in the series finale, striking out five times, and became the first Yankee to post that record since captain Aaron Judge did so during his slump in 2024. Jones struggled at the plate, prompting multiple fan reactions to his performance.
Here are some fan reactions to Jones' five-strikeout night:
"We can't have this October is around the corner," one fan commented.
"Another bust lol," another fan commented.
The Yankees lost 5-4 in extra innings, missing the chance to secure the sweep in Minnesota. The Bombers fell further in the race for the AL East crown and are now 4.5 games behind the divisional leaders, the Tampa Bay Rays.
Spencer Jones Also Had a Couple of Errors During the Twins Series
On Wednesday night, Jones failed to catch a simple fly ball to center field, allowing Kody Clemens to reach second base. Carlos Rodon showed no visible reaction to the play.
Earlier in the series opener on Monday night, Jones committed a defensive error in left-center field when the ball dipped under his glove, allowing the Twins to score two runs at the plate and prompting a frustrated reaction from starting pitcher Will Warren.
While it might have been a topsy-turvy series for the rookie outfielder, he has ensured that he is worthy of being on the active roster as October baseball nears, with 10 games left in the regular season.

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees are now in wait-and-see mode.
Aaron Judge left Wednesday’s game early with right leg tightness. There’s no word yet on whether he’ll have to miss time, and we likely won’t have an answer until Friday at the earliest.
Before then, let’s answer some of your Yankees questions in part one of our mailbag. If you want to ask anything else, there’s still time to do so here.
Note: Questions have been edited for clarity and brevity.
Advertisement
Assuming Trent Grisham is healthy, who starts in center field during the playoffs: him or Spencer Jones? — Ed H.
Yankees manager Aaron Boone told reporters Wednesday that Grisham is running “up to a decent speed” in his comeback from a right hamstring strain. Considering Grisham at normal speed is slow, it’s anyone’s guess what that actually means.
If Grisham is ready to go, it will be interesting to see what Boone decides. There are numerous examples of the Yankees opting for the veteran over an inexperienced player like Jones when the games matter most.
Both players have their warts. Neither Grisham nor Jones is a good defensive center fielder. Jones looked abysmal in center, letting a ground ball go under his glove, dropping a fly ball that hit his glove and nearly trucking Heliot Ramos in right field. Meanwhile, Grisham has trouble getting to balls over his head and in the gaps because he’s slow-footed. There’s likely a higher floor of success, though, for Grisham. Even on the balls Jones has caught, there have been instances where he doesn’t look comfortable reading the play off the bat.
So the main difference will come down to offense.
Before Grisham injured his hamstring, he was not hitting. Calls for Jones to take over were already happening. To Jones’ credit, he has produced at the plate. Even after a dreadful 0-for-6 performance with five strikeouts on Wednesday, Jones has a 113 wRC+. He is always a threat to pop a home run, and that wins ballgames in October.
Grisham has one of the best eyes on the team, rarely strikes out and works at-bats. That matters when the batters behind him would likely be Ben Rice and Judge (depending on his health).
Not that my opinion holds any weight, but I’d stick with Jones in center field. The Yankees can always use Grisham, who’s one of the most clutch hitters on the team, in big spots off the bench.
Advertisement
What will/should the Yankees playoff rotation and bullpen look like? I hate to say it, but Gerrit Cole and Max Fried are not looking like aces these days. The team is winning Will Warren’s and Carlos Rodón’s starts. How are these facts likely to influence Boone’s postseason rotation decisions? … As soon as I say this, Fried pitches a gem. Jinx. — Aaron D.
The American League East race isn’t over yet, but the likeliest outcome is the Yankees will play in a wild-card series against the Boston Red Sox. That means the Yankees will only need three starting pitchers for the first round.
Cam Schlittler should start Game 1. There’s no argument otherwise. Schlittler is one of the very best starting pitchers in the sport. You want your best pitcher going in Game 1 to give yourself the best possible chance of not facing a must-win Game 2.
From there, it’ll be a toss-up between Fried and Cole. Both pitchers have concerns attached to them.
Fried has battled command issues all season, while Cole has allowed plenty of hard contact while not getting much swing-and-miss. I’d lean toward Fried over Cole.
As for the bullpen, the Yankees could have Rodón in case the club needs length. The others likely to be on the roster are Will Warren, David Bednar, Brent Headrick, Paul Blackburn, John Schreiber, Clarke Schmidt, Ryan Yarbrough and Ryan Weathers, if he’s healthy. I’d leave off Tim Hill, who has struggled mightily this season, Luis Gil and Michael Fulmer.
What is the realistic outlook for second base next year? Jazz Chisholm Jr. hasn’t played up to his talent, which might make him more enticing by bringing down his cost. The infield is already crowded, though, with Ryan McMahon under contract, George Lombard Jr.’s promotion, José Caballero, two first basemen (three if Paul Goldschmidt is still seen as Giancarlo Stanton insurance), and Anthony Volpe’s re-ascension. — Marco F.
What the Yankees decide to do at second base is one of the most fascinating storylines of the offseason.
Advertisement
I agree with you, Marco, that this season has likely cost Chisholm millions. He is nearing the end of his worst offensive season since 2021. He won’t reach the heights he set for himself entering 2026, but he still could reach a 20-40 season. Few players have the talent to post those numbers. Before this year, Chisholm posted back-to-back 4+ fWAR seasons. It would not be wrong for the Yankees or another team to bet on his upside.
Chisholm still offers tremendous defense at second and excellent baserunning. If his bat gets back to being considerably above average, he profiles as one of the best second basemen in the sport. There are valid concerns about his offense, though. His hit tool is considerably below average, and as he ages and loses athleticism, that could be a major problem that he cannot overcome.
The Yankees should consider giving Chisholm a short-term deal, though. He is a better option than Caballero and Volpe, who are better as role players, and few available players are better than what he can provide.
The Yankees should strongly consider playing Caballero or Volpe, who played a few games in the minors there, at third base. McMahon is one of the worst everyday regulars in the big leagues this season, and there’s a higher likelihood of Caballero or Volpe producing at the plate.
Has the Martian played his last game in a Yankees uniform? — oconnell13
It’s a hard question to answer because you can’t predict injuries. You never know if the Yankees will have to reach into the minor leagues for depth.
But it’s not far-fetched to think Jasson Domínguez will never play in another important game for the Yankees again. He cannot be trusted in the field. Every game matters for the Yankees, and there’s always a queasy feeling when the ball is hit his way.
His bat also hasn’t progressed enough to keep giving him chances to prove himself. Jones has leapfrogged him on the depth chart, and the Yankees now have Heliot Ramos on their roster. There may not be space for Domínguez.
Advertisement
What are the Yankees’ pitching plans for the rest of the regular season? Specifically, who’s lining up for the Rays series and will any of them be limited in terms of pitch count? — Nick B.
As of now, the Yankees are lined up to start their best four starters against the Rays next week. Here’s how it looks:
Tuesday: Fried and Rodón are in line to start the games of the doubleheader.
Wednesday: Cole
Thursday: Schlittler
The Rays are also on track to start their best pitchers for that series. They could start Nick Martinez and Drew Rasmussen on Tuesday, Freddy Peralta on Wednesday and Ian Seymour on Thursday. Their rotation is dependent on what they decide to do for their weekend series against the Boston Red Sox. But if they wanted, all of these pitchers could factor into their pitching plans next week.
Any chance the Yanks consider Ben Rice as the backup catcher on the postseason roster to free up an extra bench spot for someone more versatile (and better than) Ali Sánchez/J.C. Escarra? — Matthew L.
The odds of this happening are close to zero.
Earlier in the season, Rice kept catching behind the scenes. Before games, he’d catch bullpens and do on-field drills with director of catching Tanner Swanson. Rice hasn’t done any of that in months.
If anything, Rice would only be used in an emergency situation. Believe it or not, the organization believes in Sánchez. That’s why they didn’t promote Mitch Garver. Sánchez is out of minor league options, so they’d have to designate him for assignment and risk him getting claimed off waivers. They value the consistency he provides to their pitchers, and they think he’s a better defender than the metrics show.

The New York Yankees already have a strong pitching staff.
Now, they'll be adding another veteran arm with less than two weeks remaining in the regular season.
On Tuesday, Gary Phillips of the New York Daily News reported that right-hander Clarke Schmidt will return from the 60-day injured list on Wednesday.
Schmidt, 30, underwent Tommy John Surgery last July and recently completed a rehab assignment.
He made five appearances between Double-A and Triple-A, throwing one to two innings at a time. According to Anthony Franco of MLB Trade Rumors, Schmidt averaged 94.1 mph on his fastball.
In all likelihood, Schmidt will be an option out of manager Aaron Boone's bullpen, not in the rotation.
New York's rotation already has a more than solid top five of Cam Schlittler, Gerrit Cole, Max Fried, Carlos Rodon, and Will Warren.
Schmidt made 14 starts in 2025 before learning surgery was required. He posted a 3.32 ERA and allowed a career-low 6.4 hits per nine innings.
To open space on the active roster, right-hander Bradley Hanner was optioned to Triple-A by the Yankees.

Baltimore, Maryland.- Paul Goldschmidt conectó un jonrón en el primer lanzamiento del partido, Trent Grisham bateó un cuadrangular de tres carreras y los Yankees de Nueva York vencieron a los Orioles de Baltimore 6-2 el martes por la noche para poner fin a una racha de cuatro derrotas consecutivas.
Will Warren (5-1) permitió dos carreras y cuatro hits en 5 2/3 entradas para los Yankees. Fue una buena actuación para el lanzador derecho, quien había permitido seis carreras en cuatro entradas a Texas en su apertura anterior.
El cuarto jonrón de apertura de Goldschmidt en su carrera y el segundo en cuatro días puso a Nueva York al frente definitivamente, y el batazo de Grisham puso el marcador 6-0 en la tercera entrada. Ambos jonrones fueron contra el zurdo Trevor Rogers, quien solo duró cuatro entradas en su regreso de la lista de lesionados tras una larga enfermedad.
En su primer partido como lanzador desde el 25 de abril, Rogers (2-4) permitió seis carreras y seis hits, elevando su efectividad a 5.77 en comparación con 1.81 en 2025.
Rogers se metió en problemas en la tercera entrada cuando otorgó dos bases por bolas consecutivas que llenaron las bases con un out. Luego, Cody Bellinger bateó un rodado que resultó en un out forzado, produciendo una carrera; Amed Rosario impulsó una carrera con un sencillo al cuadro y Grisham coronó la remontada con su sexto jonrón.
Esa ofensiva fue más que suficiente para asegurar a Nueva York su décima victoria en 11 partidos contra Baltimore, remontándonos a la temporada pasada.
Los equipos lograron superar las cuatro revisiones de decisiones arbitrales que presentaron ante el árbitro principal, Hunter Wendelstedt.
Los Yankees de Nueva York llamaron al campocorto Anthony Volpe de la filial Triple-A de Scranton/Wilkes-Barre y colocaron a José Caballero en la lista de lesionados de 10 días por una fractura en un dedo. Se espera que Volpe sea titular en el último partido de la serie el miércoles.
A continuación
El partido del miércoles se adelantó a las 13:05 h desde las 18:35 h debido a la amenaza de mal tiempo. Max Fried (4-2, 2.91 ERA) será el abridor por Nueva York, y Kyle Bradish (1-5, 4.83) será el probable abridor por Baltimore.
